prompt:
Lattice Robotics has eight autonomous pallet-moving robots in paid pilots at two warehouses and a contract to deliver 200 more across six sites over the next nine months. The pilot robots use Ubuntu, ROS 2, and a commercial x86 compute module that the five-person software team knows well. Navigation, fleet communication, diagnostics, and the 20 ms motion-control loop all run on that module; a separate certified safety controller handles emergency stops. Under synthetic CPU and network stress, the motion loop has missed its deadline in 0.4% of cycles, and one test robot came within centimeters of a rack before the safety controller stopped it. No one was hurt and no inventory was damaged.

The compute-module supplier has announced end of life in eleven months, and Lattice can buy only thirty more units. A firmware lead proposes replacing the entire onboard stack with a vendor's niche real-time operating system on a custom ARM board. The vendor projects deterministic scheduling and a $420 lower unit cost, but no one at Lattice has shipped that stack, several camera and lidar drivers would need to be built, and the first custom-board revision would arrive in five months. The manufacturing lead instead proposes keeping ROS 2 and Linux for navigation and fleet functions, moving only motion control to an industrial microcontroller, and qualifying a stocked pin-compatible compute module. That approach adds a processor boundary and saves only $90 per unit.

The pilots have accumulated 1,600 robot-hours in clean, climate-controlled buildings. The production sites include cold rooms, dust, voltage sags, intermittent wireless coverage, and maintenance crews who cannot rely on Lattice engineers to swap parts at the bench. A robot fault can injure a worker, damage inventory, or halt a customer's aisle for hours. The contract permits staged deliveries for safety validation, but mechanical and electrical configuration must be frozen in six weeks to reserve factory capacity. Write a technical foundation decision memo for Lattice's leadership that chooses the control and compute foundation for the first production run and states what later evidence, if any, should cause the company to change course.
criteria: The memo makes engineering-for-leverage primary, names the six-week hardware freeze and safe production delivery as the binding constraints, and explicitly selects the split familiar Linux/ROS 2 plus industrial-microcontroller foundation for the first production run rather than committing the run to an unproven whole-stack RTOS and custom-board rewrite.

The memo requires representative evidence from fabricated preproduction units under production motion loads, cold, dust, voltage sag, wireless loss, long-duration operation, assembly variation, and field-maintenance conditions; it sets binary limits for control-loop deadline misses, safe stops, recovery, and operability on a hardware-appropriate weeks-or-months cadence rather than accepting synthetic benchmarks or eight clean pilots as sufficient.

The memo defines a narrow, testable boundary between hard-real-time motion control and Linux-hosted navigation or fleet functions, preserves the independent certified emergency-stop path, and requires interface or invariant tests, fail-safe behavior during processor or link failure, diagnosable state, update and rollback handling, and a behavior-preserving migration from the pilot robots.

The memo compares both foundations over their full lifecycle, including component availability and exit risk, board and certification work, driver and library maturity, team proficiency and hiring, debugging, deployment, observability, security, manufacturing test, field service, maintenance, schedule, and unit cost; it treats the projected RTOS determinism and savings as assumptions and permits a later custom platform only if representative evidence shows durable net product leverage over the capable split baseline.

The memo records a named engineering owner, decision and review dates, precommitted keep or switch thresholds, rejected alternatives and remaining uncertainty, a portability or fallback seam for the compute module, and explicit branches that preserve staged production if evidence disappoints; it leaves any customer-visible deployment and exposure gate to shipping-and-iterating-products after the internal foundation meets its technical and safety thresholds.
